Area.evidence_source: It is important to keep the spiritual/religious dimension in mind as we assess people who are at risk for suicidal behaviour and also in planning suicide prevention programmes in Ghana. Already, religious groups have become very active in the delivery of health care (Roberts, 2001). However, it is important to be mindful of judgmental attitudes and possible abuse within the religious system. For example, Roberts (2001) documented that in some prayer and faith camps in Ghana, persons who are ill are chained or beaten so as to exorcise evil spirits from them. Additionally, the judgmental attitude would scare people away from seeking help. In order to be able to fully exploit the help of the religious leaders we thus need proper education of them as well. Providing training and education to religious leaders in Ghana regarding risk factors for suicide and religious coping cannot be overemphasised. There are indications that religious groups are already offering mental health services including counselling, outlets for rehabilitation and prayers for those with mental health challenges in the country (Ae-Ngibise et al., 2010; Atindanbila & Thompson, 2011). Religious leaders can work together with other professionals in the field of mental health to provide support to those who are going through suicidal crisis. Additionally, religious bodies should be encouraged to initiate and maintain church programmes that would provide various kinds of services to those identified as having challenges and are unable to cope effectively (Osafo et al., 2013). Due to the lack of mental health professionals in Ghana, the Government has recognised the contribution to mental health service provision that can be played by religious leaders and groups and is working to improve such services and incorporate them into the formal mental health-care system (WHO, 2007). The indication that religious groups are engaging in some form of mental health care and the attempt by government to formally integrate their services into mental health-care delivery in the country could be an initial step in task shifting in suicide prevention. Task shifting, the process of delegating tasks to health workers with lower qualifications but capable of doing the task reliably, or between different groups of professional workers or from professional to lay health workers (McParke & Mensah, 2008) is quite necessary in Ghana considering that there are few mental health professionals in the country. In summary, religious institutions are helping in providing mental health care in Ghana and if properly equipped with further knowledge through training could play an important role in suicide prevention.
